channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: ROSTR Launches Free Global Database of 33,000 Music Venues
item.description: Hypebot: “Independent live music trade and technology company The ROSTR Group has launched ROSTR Venues, a sweeping new live music directory. Covering over 33,000 venues across North America (13,000+), Europe (10,000+), and Latin America (9,000+), this interactive map and database aims to make booking a gig as intuitive as booking an Airbnb.”

item.title: CM Fadnavis Launches Bappa.org Digital Archive to Preserve Ganeshotsav Heritage
item.description: Indiatimes: “Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis launchedBappa.org – Gatha Ganesh-kathanchi, a digital archive documenting Ganeshotsav traditions from nearly40,000 villagesacross the state. He said the platform will preserve local customs, stories, and cultural heritage while making them accessible globally.” The site is available in English.

item.title: Department of Fire Services Launches Hot Work Violation Database
item.description: State of Massachusetts: “The Department of Fire Services has launched a new, public-facing database to document violations of the State Fire Code and Massachusetts General Laws regarding welding, grinding, and other hot work processes.”

item.title: VGHF Digital Archive passes 5000 magazines. Here’s what’s next.
item.description: Video Game History Foundation: “Our magazine library now spans 46 years of video game history, from 1981–2026. Major new additions since launch include hundreds of trade magazines, a historically significant newsletter, and publications for niche gaming communities. Altogether, these account for about 60 percent of the Video Game History Foundation’s entire physical magazine collection that we’ve cataloged so far.”

item.title: PewDiePie ends family vlogs on YouTube after promising to focus on son’s privacy
item.description: Dextero: “Over the last few years, PewDiePie has ceased making the gaming videos that brought him to popularity. The Swedish content creator is still synonymous with YouTube, but has changed his content to be more focused on real-life happenings. In that, he started uploading monthly vlogs talking about his new life with family in Japan, discussing other projects he was working on outside of YouTube, and documenting the growth of his son, Bjorn.”

item.title: The World Drawn by 3,000 People
item.description: Maps Mania: “The object of Borderline is very simple. You are shown a map without borders and asked to draw the outline of a named country. You are then scored on the accuracy of your drawn border. The scoring appears to be based on two measures of accuracy.”

item.title: How online toxicity silences the majority and fuels power users
item.description: PsyPost: “In online political discussions, a small fraction of highly active users typically generates the vast majority of content while most people silently observe. A recent experiment reveals that polite and constructive environments encourage silent readers to post their first comment, but the most active users are driven to post more when discussions become toxic. These findings were published in the journal Science Advances.”

item.title: UC Berkeley researchers create digital twin of Pajaro Valley to test future flood risks
item.description: Local News Matters Bay Area: “THE FARMING COMMUNITIES along the Lower Pajaro River that divides Monterey and Santa Cruz counties have suffered five multi-million dollar floods since a system of levees was built in 1949. Now, researchers are building a dynamic virtual version of the region to simulate flooding scenarios over time, while taking account of a variety of factors such as climate risk.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Important New Resource: All 24 volumes of the important journal Jewish Art, formerly the Journal of Jewish Art, have been digitalized and made freely available for download
item.description: Jewish Heritage Europe: “All 24 volumes of the important journal Jewish Art, formerly the Journal of Jewish Art (1974-1985), have been digitalized and made freely available for download on the web site of the Center for Jewish Art.”

item.title: Flipbook
item.description: Spotted on LinkedIn: From the backstory: “It takes any IIIF manifest as input (it also takes plain item links from digital collections sites), and adds the item to your ‘shelf’ which persists in your browser storage. You can ‘scrub’ back and forth through a sample of the pages, and hopefully get a sense of what lies between the covers.”

item.title: Introducing the AAMies: AAM Innovative Exhibition Showcase
item.description: American Alliance of Museums: “Part exhibition design challenge, part science fair, and part friendly competition, the AAMies are designed to celebrate what our field does best: turning big ideas into meaningful experiences visitors can actually have. And yes, there will be trophies. More specifically, the Golden Stanchion. [A Stannie! — TJC] Each year, the AAMies will pose a challenge to the museum field around an issue where exhibitions – the distinctly human, physical, place-based experiences museums create – can make an impact.”

item.title: Google seemingly confirms plans to kill ChromeOS in 2034
item.description: Ars Technica: “We are mere days away from the launch of Googlebooks, the long-awaited Android laptops that Google hopes will compete with macOS and Windows. But what of Chromebooks? There have been hints that Google plans to sunset its web-first ChromeOS platform, and a new support page lays out some of the specifics.”

item.title: Comics Creators And Readers Are Reeling After The News That Tapas Is Shutting Down
item.description: Kotaku: “Tapas, a popular North American comic and web novel hosting site, is shutting down. According to a report on BigGo Finance, Tapas is ‘a drag on earnings’ for parent company Kakao Entertainment, a South Korean media company which purchased the platform in 2021 for roughly $800 million. BigGo Finance reports that Tapas was home to over ‘100,000 titles’ from ‘75,000 creators’ and had amassed over ’10 million cumulative registered users,’ many of whom are upset right now.”

item.title: Private List Warns Woman of “Over a Hundred” Allegedly Predatory Men in Silicon Valley
item.description: Futurism: “The list, on top of names, is said to contain details of alleged acts of abuse which include drugging, sexual assaults, and rape. But it’s very selectively distributed, probably in part to protect the people who’ve made the allegations.”

item.title: A ‘freaked out’ US food industry is hitting back at Maga – with social media influencers
item.description: The Guardian: “Some of the biggest food and agriculture corporations in the US are funding a campaign that pays social media influencers to combat elements of Robert F Kennedy Jr’s Make America Healthy Again platform, according to an investigation by the Guardian and Documented, an investigative watchdog and journalism project.”

item.title: Google challenges EU orders to open up to AI, search-engine rivals
item.description: Reuters: “Google has challenged two EU orders to help AI rivals such as OpenAI access its services and ​search engine competitors to access its search data, saying these would undermine ‌privacy safeguards and cause irreversible harm to European users.”

item.title: Elon Musk, SpaceXAI subpoenaed by NYC in AI safety investigation
item.description: CNBC: “The New York City Council issued a subpoena on Monday to Elon Musk, requiring that he or another representative of SpaceXAI testify in an investigation concerning artificial intelligence safety risks.”

item.title: Museum leaders call for ‘transformation, not incremental change’
item.description: Museums Journal: “Museum leaders are seeking ‘transformation, not incremental change’, according to a report published this week by Arts Council England (ACE). The Museums Overview 2026 found that England’s museums face “severe financial pressures”, along with workforce shortages and increasingly unsustainable approaches to collections management.”

item.title: Risks faced by teens online vary by platform, study shows
item.description: University of Southern California: “A recent study in JAMA Pediatrics describes a pioneering assessment of how different online platforms expose teens to different types of harm. USC researchers collaborated on the Stanford University-led study with New York University colleagues and analyzed data from 472 teens ages 13 to 17 who participated in USC’s Understanding America Survey.”

item.title: 127 year-old fly launches major digitisation project in Scotland
item.description: National Museums Scotland: “As Scotland’s Climate Week gets underway, a 127 year-old hoverfly is among the first insect specimens to be digitised as part of a major new project led in Scotland by National Museums Scotland and Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New website/app crowd sources stock of supplies at stores across Hawaiʻi before, during, after storms
item.description: Big Island Now: “With ongoing storms impacting Hawaiʻi this year, a computer engineer in Pāhoa has created a website to help residents quickly find supplies. After Hurricane Lala severely damaged parts of the Big Island, Sean Repanshek, 34, reached out to friends across the island to assess their well-being and inquire about their preparation experiences.”

item.title: When disaster strikes, newsrooms scramble. A new website aims to help tame the chaos.
item.description: NiemanLab: “Emergency Mode’s website has pre-made checklists for various kinds of extreme weather disasters, like hurricanes, wildfires, or extreme heat, written by journalists who have experience covering those types of disasters. The website also links to Grist’s disaster toolkit and has a module to help create an ‘action pack’ with resources that change depending on whether the journalists coming to the site are preparing for a threat ahead of time, in the midst of an emergency, or recovering from a disaster.”

item.title: NOAA’s flood mapping tool now covers nearly 100% of U.S.
item.description: NOAA: “NOAA’s National Weather Service announced today that Flood Inundation Mapping (FIM), a revolutionary tool for predicting river flooding, is now available on an experimental basis to nearly 100% of the U.S. population. This is a massive expansion from FIM’s prior coverage of 60% of the country.”

item.title: Cyber Law Toolkit releases 2026 update and opens call for new scenarios
item.description: University of Exeter: “The Cyber Law Toolkit is a global online platform showing crucial information about international law and the cyber activities of nations. It offers a unique combination of resources, including detailed hypothetical scenarios, a repository of real-world cyber incidents, and a comprehensive collection of national positions on international law in cyberspace.”

item.title: Google celebrates its 28th birthday with nostalgic doodle – how did the search engine mark earlier milestones?
item.description: London Standard: “Today is Google’s 28th birthday – and the search engine is marking the milestone with a very nostalgic doodle. The tech titan paid tribute to itself with a doodle from its early years.”

item.title: CSUN Gets Grant to Digitize Its Collection of Images by Pioneering Photographer Vera Jackson
item.description: CSUN: “Her photos captured life in Black Los Angeles during the 1940s and ’50s. Vera Jackson, the only woman who worked in the 1940s as a staff photographer for The California Eagle — the oldest Black newspaper — captured images of weddings, society events and protests, chronicling every-day life in a community that was largely ignored by the rest of the city. The John Randolph Hayes and Dora Hayes Foundation has awarded California State University, Northridge nearly $70,000 to digitize Jackson’s work and make it available to the public through the Tom & Ethel Bradley Center’s digital collection in CSUN’s University Library.”

item.title: White House Drove Users to Official App Fraught With Trackers
item.description: Washington Sun: “No one can say definitively where the user data ends up. But it’s clear the White House app covertly collects excessive user data and shares it with third-party trackers while sidestepping federal security rules, according to cybersecurity experts and an independent risk assessment conducted by The Washington Sun.”

item.title: This Meta Muse incident is a scary warning about trusting AI agents
item.description: Android Authority: “Threads user Matt Robb shared what happened after using Muse to handle a Facebook Marketplace listing. According to screenshots he posted, the AI negotiated with a buyer, agreed to a price, shared his address, and arranged a pickup — all without him realizing someone had actually been invited over.”

item.title: PsyPost deploys audit program to track retracted and corrected scientific studies in its archive
item.description: PsyPost: “PsyPost, a psychology and neuroscience news website, has implemented a new automated Python program designed to monitor its archive for scientific studies that have been retracted, corrected, or flagged by publishers.”

item.title: When did Google get so f-ing weird?
item.description: Sancho Panza’s Thoughts: “Google, a search engine which does not have human emotions, assumed that I had been spurned by a man in my life named Dario and decided what I wanted was an empathetic digital friend. What I wanted was some links, but that’s not what Google does in 2026.”

item.title: Dolly Parton’s ‘9 to 5’ Returns to Theaters With Ticket Sales Donated to Dollywood Foundation After Star’s Death
item.description: Variety: “Dolly Parton‘s hit 1980 comedy ‘9 to 5’ will return to theaters next month for one week in the wake of the country superstar’s death on Aug. 25 at age 80. All U.S. ticket sales will be donated to The Dollywood Foundation to support its flagship program, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: 140 million pages of knowledge history accessible online: Four Swiss libraries launch the platform «Books as Data»
item.description: From University of Basel, and machine-translated from German: “The platform ‘Books as Data’ makes the holdings of four academic libraries from the years 1700 to 1900 fully accessible and searchable. In addition to scholarly literature, the collection includes journals and fiction from Switzerland, Europe, and around the world – a representative part of Switzerland’s knowledge landscape during this period.”

item.title: Revamped Data Tool IDs Trends In Mental Health, Substance Use Among CT Residents
item.description: CT News Junkie: “The portal is designed to provide researchers, journalists, and community members statewide with streamlined access to mental health and substance use data through interactive visualizations and centralized resources.”

item.title: Made On YouTube 2026
item.description: Google Blog: “Made On YouTube is the yearly event where we show you the latest product launches and platform improvements that creators and viewers will use and see on YouTube in the coming year.”

item.title: After the Flood Came the Lies
item.description: The Assembly (NC): “Disinformation—the deliberate spreading of falsehoods—about malicious intentions or neglect on the part of emergency management agencies became one of the key storylines after Helene. Debunking rumors added strain to an overburdened agency communications apparatus… and clogged social media, taking attention away from the lifesaving information people needed.”

item.title: Club Cobra’s Instagram page returns after 9-month battle with Meta
item.description: Q Voice News: “In a one-two punch, A.I.-driven search engines listed his clubs as permanently closed. Longtime regulars texted him condolences. Then, by June 1, approximately a dozen Instagram pages from his staff and affiliated club promoters had been suspended. Again, nobody received a warning or explanation about why the pages were turned off.”

item.title: VLC has a hidden live TV feature, and it gives you thousands of free channels
item.description: MakeUseOf: “The second part of the puzzle is knowing where you can find the free TV channels, and this is where IPTV-org comes in. It is one of those open-source projects that can replace something you’d normally pay for, except in this case, it replaces cable TV.” I use Ubuntu so I already had VLC. I tried this and wow! You might get confused by an error message saying something didn’t load. That was probably an URL on the video playlist. Follow the instructions to find the playlist.

item.title: Museums and Climate: Why Cultural Institutions Belong in the Conversation
item.description: MuseumNext: “…museums are not just commentators. Their buildings, exhibitions and supply chains carry a real environmental footprint, which gives them the chance to lead by example. Here are four ways museums around the world are proving that cultural institutions belong in the climate conversation.”

item.title: Researchers to conduct first comprehensive archaeological study of extreme medieval sports
item.description: University of Exeter: “The medieval tournament – the iconic chivalric spectacle of jousting and mock battles – is to be the focus of a first-ever comprehensive archaeological study. The 30-month project at the University of Exeter will break new ground in exploring some of the locations and landscapes that staged these ‘extreme sports’ of the Middle Ages.”

item.title: Negative feelings about life are more common among teens on Instagram and TikTok
item.description: PsyPost: “A recent survey of teenagers suggests that a large portion of young people encounter negative experiences on the internet, and the types of harm they face tend to vary depending on which apps they use.”

item.title: Robot Makes Literal Daisy Chains
item.description: Hackaday: “[Jude Robinson]’s robot Daisy has an unusual function: making a literal chain of daisies. The device is his student final project and demonstrates how a system can replace sensing with clever mechanical constraints. Instead of bringing tools to bear on each daisy, the daisies are brought to the tools in a repeatable, deterministic way.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: ChatGPT Helped Tumbler Ridge Shooter Focus on Guns, Tactics, and Terror
item.description: Mother Jones: “The violent contents of Van Rootselaar’s two ChatGPT accounts, detailed here publicly for the first time, are far more extensive and disturbing than previously known. Van Rootselaar, who was 18 at the time of the attack, also used OpenAI’s chatbot to upload bloody images of extreme violence and photos of harm to herself. She pushed ChatGPT to create graphic fictional narratives of mass killings. One featured an 18-year-old perpetrator who livestreamed a mass shooting that went viral and, in ChatGPT’s telling, made her an online ‘legend.'”

item.title: Maga base recoils as Donald Trump goes all-in on AI
item.description: Financial Times: “On January 6 2021, Amy Kremer stood near the White House, urging Maga supporters to ‘Stop the Steal’ of the election from Donald Trump. Now she is again rallying the president’s fans — this time to join a revolt against his pro-AI agenda. ‘I’m not a sheep, I don’t just blindly follow,’ Kremer, a former Tea Party activist who founded Women for Trump, told a crowd gathered for an AI data centre protest in West Virginia’s solidly Republican Berkeley County last week.”

item.title: Data Centers Are Driving Up Ohio Electric Bills, Whether or Not They Get Built
item.description: Columbus Underground: “Utilities base their grid investments on demand projections. In Ohio, those forecasts are now through the roof. The state’s largest regulated electric utility is American Electric Power’s Ohio Power Co., which anticipates demand will nearly triple over the next decade, largely due to expected data center projects. Critics question the validity of these forecasts — and the wisdom of using them to justify costly investments that utility customers will end up on the hook for if the numbers don’t pan out.”

item.title: Are Black Residents Being Left Out of Atlanta’s Data Center Talks?
item.description: Capital B Atlanta: “In only a few years, Atlanta has become one of the fastest-growing markets for data center development in the country. In the first half of 2026, the city had the most data center space under construction in the U.S. It’s the first time the city has surpassed Northern Virginia, which has been called ‘Data Center Alley.'”

item.title: Classified Estimates Show the NSA Is Paying Billions to Test AI Models
item.description: Washington Sun: “The National Security Agency told lawmakers that it is spending billions of dollars in taxpayer funds this year evaluating and testing advanced artificial intelligence models, according to two sources familiar with classified intelligence estimates. The price tag — which is significantly greater than previously known — has led lawmakers to believe that a more comprehensive AI regulatory system could cost the government tens of billions of dollars per year, the sources said.”

item.title: NJ fines data center $1 million for illegally powering facility with gas generators
item.description: Gothamist: “The Sherrill administration has fined a large data center in New Jersey over $1 million for installing and operating 62 large gas powered generators without state permits. The penalty comes as growth of the data center industry, and the energy it requires, has been blamed for rising electricity prices in the state and sparked environmental concerns.”

item.title: Battle of Hospital A.I. vs. Insurer A.I. Is Pushing Medical Costs Higher
item.description: New York Times: “In the latest sign that artificial intelligence is fueling higher health care costs, a group of insurers released a report Thursday claiming that hospitals’ use of A.I. was responsible for nearly $1 billion in additional expenses over two years.”

item.title: China’s ‘Lipstick King’ confronts slower growth, AI disruption in livestream shopping
item.description: Reuters: “For nearly a decade, China’s ‘Lipstick King’ has been the face of the livestream shopping industry, helping to grow a niche format into one of ​the country’s most important retail channels. Now, despite slowing growth and artificial intelligence reshaping the sector, Li Jiaqi, famed for selling billions of dollars ‌worth of beauty products to more than 100 million followers, bets it will still depend on people like him.”

item.title: AI-generated influencers targeting FIFO workers to sell online adult content
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “When she is not on site commenting on the quality of the food served up at the mess hall, she is an avid West Coast Eagles supporter going to the football, or soaking up the sun on Perth’s Cottesloe Beach. There is just one problem: Bindi Raye does not exist. Her face, voice and online persona are a generative AI fabrication.”

item.title: Unsecured OpenAI agents posted 53 user images on the internet without the lab’s knowledge
item.description: TechCrunch: “After images that users uploaded to OpenAI models were included in training data, AI agents operating in the company’s research environment posted them on public image hosting sites.”

item.title: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
item.description: CNBC: “The release on Monday of Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.”

item.title: AI-generated ‘experts’ make up large network of German political videos
item.description: Euronews: “Researchers identified 47 YouTube channels using artificial presenters to discuss conflicts, geopolitics and German politics, with videos recording more than 7.5 million views.”

item.title: Doubtful about Muse AI, so far
item.description: Tim Boucher: “Have been doing a trial of FB’s Muse AI app for Mac desktop. And call me old-fashioned but in my time we didn’t ask for full disk access on the first date, along with credit card verification, and no expiring chats. You can deny it full disk access and still seemingly have it run things on its cloud virtual machine (VM), but you can’t assign it individual folder access like you can with ChatGPT Work/Codex, which I have also been testing and enjoying a lot more than Muse.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Texture launches CommonGrid, an open source registry of the US power grid
item.description: PR Newswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “Built and moderated like Wikipedia, CommonGrid connects every U.S. electric utility, grid operator, power plant, and major asset into a single structured model, where every change is attributed to a contributor, cited to a source, timestamped, and reversible. A grid model this large stays accurate only if the people who work on it can fix it, which is why CommonGrid is built to be corrected rather than published once.”

item.title: Deep mining for memories: Greece opens digital archive to preserve Serifos ironworks history
item.description: Euronews: “The digital archive (source in Greek)contains more than 250 photographs, rare documents, press clippings from the period and 10 first-hand testimonies by miners and their descendants who are still alive. This was deemed necessary because for decades the history of the Serifos mines survived mainly through the oral accounts of those who had lived and worked there.”

item.title: New Mexico jury finds Facebook liable of deceiving users about privacy protections
item.description: Associated Press: “A New Mexico jury on Friday found Facebook liable for deceiving users about privacy protections on the platform in the latest legal setback against the social media giant that has already cost it billions of dollars. The jury found over 43 million violations of state consumer protection law and it is now up to the judge to determine how much the company would pay, with attorneys representing the state asking for the maximum $5,000 penalty per violation.”

item.title: WordPress 7.1.2 Release
item.description: WordPress: “This security release features a fix for a critical severity security vulnerability. Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.”

item.title: YouTube and Meta Reverse Course, Will Accept ‘Musk’ Trailer Ad
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Bleecker Street, the studio behind Alex Gibney’s upcoming Musk, will be allowed to buy an ad for the trailer on the platform after all, a YouTube spokesperson tells The Hollywood Reporter. The trailer ‘was temporarily restricted by our system. Following review, the ad has been cleared to run,’ the company said, also posting the message to social media. Meanwhile, a Meta spokesperson tells THR that a decision to reject the ad ‘was an error and we’re restoring the ads.'” Sure Jan. lol.

item.title: Make your website printable – a short guide
item.description: Juha-Matti Santala: “Have you ever printed a web page or thought about how your website looks like if someone were to print it? Let this short guide provide you a starting point on your journey to make the reader’s experience better if they decide to print your page.”

item.title: Bard College Launches Ralph Ellison Center, Establishing a Permanent Home for Ellison’s Literary and Intellectual Legacy
item.description: Bard College: “Having inherited the rights to the Ralph Ellison archive at the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., the Center will embark on an ambitious digitization project to advance the tools scholars use to engage in research on Ellison and create a digital archive that enables the sharing of knowledge with other academic and cultural institutions and the general public.”

item.title: Interior Ministry now publishes deceased people’s personal data online
item.description: ERR: “Since mid-September, Estonia’s Interior Ministry has been issuing a table of personal data on people who have died in the past 100 years, replacing individual queries. The dataset on andmed.eesti.ee includes personal identification codes, names and dates of birth and death for people born from 1926 onwards.”

item.title: ShinyHunters hackers say they stole psychiatric and medical records of FBI staff
item.description: Reuters: “FBI personnel data recently stolen by the ShinyHunters hackers includes sensitive psychiatric and medical ​evaluation records, according to the hackers and documents reviewed by Reuters.”

item.title: Academic publisher Elsevier hit by LAPSUS$ redirect attack
item.description: The Register: “Academic publishing giant Elsevier confirmed a compromise this week after students found its platform redirecting users to a cybercriminal crew’s leak page.”

item.title: AAM Supports Congressional Action to Protect the Smithsonian’s Independence
item.description: American Alliance of Museums: “The American Alliance of Museums (AAM) endorses The Smithsonian Integrity and Historical Independence Act of 2026, introduced by Representatives Stanbury (D-NM), Jackson (D-IL), and Mfume (D-MD), which would protect the scholarly independence of the Smithsonian Institution from political influence.”

item.title: Fifth of News UK website traffic was ‘non-human’ in past six months
item.description: Press Gazette: “About a fifth of all News UK traffic in the last six months was non-human, chief technology officer Tom Jackson has revealed. But he said bot attacks were even higher before it deployed new bot protection technology which has made its sites ‘less of a target’.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Introducing: the EU Agriculture and Climate Dashboard
item.description: Institute for Agriculture & Trade Policy: “The Dashboard explores key aspects of the intersection between agriculture and climate change, drawing together publicly available data in illustrated form to show where EU countries are making progress — or falling short — on agriculture and climate goals. The Dashboard compiles data that’s previously been difficult to access across an array of various reports, charts, and websites, bringing it together into one central hub of information.”

item.title: IAFF launches new Resource Library for health and safety
item.description: International Association of Fire Fighters: “The IAFF has launched a new Resource Library, a single online hub for nearly 300 – and counting – health and safety resources for fire fighters and emergency medical workers. The new tool puts the information members need to protect themselves and serve their communities directly in their hands.”

item.title: New leadership for British Library as cyber attack recovery continues
item.description: Museums Association: “Former UK Space Agency chief Paul Bate will take over the leadership of the British Library in November, as the institution continues its recovery from the 2023 cyber attack. Bate, who succeeds interim chief executive Jeremy Silver, will take up the role on 4 November after five years as chief executive of the UK Space Agency.”

item.title: Club Cobra’s Instagram page returns after 9-month battle with Meta
item.description: Q Voice News: “A nine-month struggle by Club Cobra, the queer Latino dance space in North Hollywood, to regain access to its Instagram page is finally over. Nightlife businessman Marty Sokol said the Instagram page for Club Cobra vanished New Year’s Day, while the page for his other space, Club Chico, a gay Latino bar in Montebello, disappeared in May, without a warning or an explanation.”

item.title: If You Ask Grok, Elon Musk Acted Like a Jackass at the Trump/Xi Dinner
item.description: Gizmodo: “President Donald Trump hosted a lavish state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday, where several U.S. oligarchs showed up to kiss the ring. Photos from the event have been circulating widely on social media, including shots of Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, and billionaire Elon Musk. But there’s one photo that has gotten a lot of attention Friday morning, and it definitely stands out for being weird.”

item.title: Owners mourn spoiled food after firmware update bricks Samsung smart fridges
item.description: Ars Technica: “Some Samsung smart fridges stopped working on Tuesday due to a firmware update. Korean outlets were the first to report the problems, which affect Samsung’s Bespoke AI line of fridges. Star News Korea, per a Google-provided translation, said that most of the affected devices were four-door fridges from 2024 or later.”

item.title: Appeals court rules that states can regulate Kalshi’s sports prediction markets, dealing another legal blow to platforms
item.description: CNBC: “The 6th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled on Friday that states have a right to regulate sports-related event contracts on prediction market platforms, marking a second major legal defeat for the industry as a fight at the U.S. Supreme Court looms.”

item.title: This guy has spent two years hunting fake job listings on LinkedIn, and found 60,000 of them
item.description: TechSpot: “Since being laid off from an advertising role in late 2023, [Jay] Jones says he has helped get nearly 60,000 fake job listings removed from the internet, most of them from LinkedIn. He has also flagged about 7,000 profiles that he believes were used in job scams.”

item.title: OAPEN and Max Planck Society partner to build collection of funded open access books
item.description: Max Planck Digital Library: “The OAPEN Foundation is delighted to announce a new partnership with the Max Planck Society (MPG) to build a dedicated collection of open access books funded by more than 80 Max Planck Institutes (MPIs) and research facilities. The Institutes and research facilities range in expertise, from natural and life sciences to the humanities. The collection will provide MPG with comprehensive oversight of open access books funded by its institutes or centrally via the Max Planck Digital Library (MPDL). Max Planck-affiliated authors will also benefit from increased dissemination of their open access books.”

item.title: Yale Library’s digitized Takamiya Collection helps solve mystery of medieval fragments
item.description: Yale Library: “The location of the missing manuscript leaves had been a mystery for nearly a century. Relying on clues from earlier scholars and archivists, Dr. Katie Walter (University of Sussex) and Dr. James Wade (Girton College, Cambridge) followed a trail that led from The Keep to Yale Library. Because the library had fully digitized the manuscript (Takamiya MS 20), Walter and Wade were able to match the loose leaves in The Keep archive with images in the library’s digital archive.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Auditor Ball Launches Online Tool to Track Public Benefit Processing Errors
item.description: State of Kentucky: “The Kentucky Auditor of Public Accounts is launching a new Public Benefit Error Rate Tracker. This online, public-facing tool will display monthly error rates and estimated wasted taxpayer dollars measured by the Ombudsman within the Beshear administration’s processing of major public benefit programs. The displayed error rates measure how often a state agency processes a public benefit case incorrectly.”

item.title: RootsTech 2027 Opens Registration with Dual In-Person and Virtual Format
item.description: Genealogy’s Star: “Registration is officially open for RootsTech 2027, scheduled for March 4–6, 2027. Hosted by FamilySearch International, the conference returns to its dual format: an in-person gathering at the Salt Palace Convention Center in Salt Lake City, Utah, alongside a free virtual program broadcast worldwide.”

item.title: Automattic has a new board after failed attempt to put CEO on leave
item.description: TechCrunch: “Automattic CEO Matt Mullenweg has rebuilt the company’s board just weeks after its previous directors tried, and failed, to oust him. The board, which was announced to staff Friday, is an eclectic group that includes a best-selling science-fiction author and two co-founders of the now-defunct social app IRL, TechCrunch has learned, and Mullenweg has confirmed.”

item.title: TikTok settles lawsuit with Alabama for at least $100 million, will implement safety features
item.description: Associated Press: “TikTok will pay the state of Alabama at least $100 million and must implement a slew of safety features for teens in the state as part of a settlement agreement reached just before the case was set to go to trial. Alabama sued the social media company in 2025 claiming that the platform had negative effects on the mental well-being of youths.”

item.title: The Major Social Media Platforms Are All Rejecting Paid Ads for Alex Gibney’s ‘Musk’ (Exclusive)
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “The studio releasing Alex Gibney’s new Elon Musk documentary Musk is finding itself unable to buy an ad on the biggest social platforms. YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram and Facebook owner Meta are all declining to run the trailer for Musk, along with X itself, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.”

item.title: A massive MTA archive ended up in a Virginia warehouse. A Brooklyn man brought it home.
item.description: Gothamist: “Archivist Daylon Orr was visiting a bookseller friend in Virginia this summer when, in the back corner of his friend’s warehouse, he noticed a giant stack of boxes labeled IRT — the acronym for Interborough Rapid Transit Company, a former private operator of what would become the New York City subway.”

item.title: Have You Seen This? YouTuber builds Chrome’s dinosaur game
item.description: KSL: “Do you remember the game with the dinosaur jumping over the cacti that can make the internet going out seem less bad, or even great in some circumstances? The disappointment when the internet returns and now you have to get back to the homework?”

item.title: Russia targets Ukraine’s data centres
item.description: Financial Times: “Russia has increased strikes on Ukrainian data centres and telecommunications facilities, disrupting internet access across Kyiv and raising concerns that Moscow is seeking to undermine Ukraine’s digital economy.”

item.title: You’ll do anything for your baby. The algorithm knows how to exploit that.
item.description: Alaska Beacon: “Bringing home a bundle of joy in America today unleashes a digital onslaught of advertisements pushing products, services and apps that target mothers most fiercely, with a clear promise: The gadget that will solve all your parenting puzzles is just a click away.”

item.title: Exclusive: Sham scientific societies are misleading star researchers
item.description: Nature: “These entities belong to a sprawling international constellation of suspicious academies and societies that have successfully misled some of the world’s leading scientists and universities, including Stanford University in California and the US National Academies of Sciences (NAS) in Washington DC. The deceptive organizations’ websites often contain content that has been plagiarized or manipulated, falsehoods about their institutional histories and locations and honorifics available for purchase. The goal for these kinds of organization, says Fan Xiudi, an educational-policy specialist at Tongji University in Shanghai, China, seems to be to build a facade of legitimacy, and then use that to sell memberships and awards to early-career researchers, particularly in China.”

item.title: Trump administration guts data collection on US education as math and reading scores plummet
item.description: The Guardian: “As reading and math scores fall to their lowest point in the past quarter-century, the US now has fewer tools to understand and develop interventions for this troubling trend. When the Trump administration took a wrecking ball to the Department of Education last year, firing nearly half of its workers and allowing the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge) to cancel nearly $900m in contracts, a little-known agency called the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) was among the hardest hit.”

item.title: Choctaw Nation celebrates the launch of new language app, Rosetta Stone partnership
item.description: KOSU: “A new Choctaw language app, created through Rosetta Stone’s Endangered Language Program, is now available at no cost through the tribe’s online portal.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Latino Virginia oral history project to get wider audience
item.description: Virginia Commonwealth University: “On Saturday, VCU’s Migration Studies Lab, part of the Humanities Research Center, is presenting the Migration Studies Research Symposium, a daylong event at the Virginia Museum of History and Culture. The program includes a preview of Latino Virginia, which has conducted more than 100 interviews so far with individuals from every Latin American country and whose roots span South and Central America, the Caribbean and Mexico.”

item.title: LinkedIn adds new tools to fight fake profiles and bogus work histories
item.description: TechCrunch: “AI has made it significantly easier for people to create fake accounts and identities to engage in online manipulation and scams. On Wednesday, LinkedIn announced a new set of tools to combat the problem while helping people and companies better control their presence on the platform.”

item.title: Elon Said Fighting CSAM Was “Priority #1.” A NY Times Reporter With A Script Found 75 Known Images.
item.description: Techdirt: “Last year there was a report that one of the major tool providers for CSAM detection, Thorn, had cut off X, because Elon refused to pay the bill. At the time, X responded angrily to anyone asking about the Thorn situation by claiming that they had put in place their own, better technology to spot CSAM. How’s that going? Not too well, according to the NY Times, which worked with the Canadian Center for Child Protection to scan X for known abuse imagery.”

item.title: How the ‘poisonous tide’ of disinformation spreads division and despair
item.description: The Guardian: “Sophie Williams-Dunning, a cyber analyst at the Royal United Services Institute (Rusi) thinktank, says there is now a ‘sophisticated ecosystem which exists to exacerbate provokable users for one reason or another’. Although Burnham is targeting ‘hostile state information attacks’, this ecosystem does not just include Russia, which likes to amplify ‘divisive content’, says Williams-Dunning.”

item.title: Traffic chaos in Perthshire villages after Google Maps glitch
item.description: BBC: “A Google Maps glitch has caused chaos after traffic was mistakenly diverted from the A9 to a single-track road between Dunkeld and Pitlochry.”

item.title: Castro LGBTQ club Beaux latest to fight Instagram deactivation
item.description: Bay Area Reporter: “More LGBTQ businesses in San Francisco have been penalized by having their social media accounts deactivated. The Bay Area Reporter first shined a light last year on allegations Meta is treating Instagram accounts linked to the LGBTQ community unfairly.”

item.title: ICE Wiped Thousands of People From Its Database. Families Are Paying the Price.
item.description: Mother Jones: “That man is one of thousands of detained immigrants with ‘Final Orders of Removal’ whose records have been hidden or deleted from ICE’s tracking system, leaving families and lawyers unable to locate them. As the Associated Press reported on Monday, those records began to vanish September 15. Thousands of people in ICE custody are likely affected.”

item.title: X now tells users when local laws have reduced their posts’ visibility
item.description: Engadget: “Social media network X has added more transparency surrounding some of its visibility practices, which could further reduce claims that the platform engages in shadowbanning. The company announced that its Under the Hood menu will now reveal if X has limited visibility for an account’s posts in compliance with local laws.”

item.title: False claims about birth control are proliferating online, KFF survey says
item.description: Idaho Capital Sun: “More than half of women of reproductive age have seen or heard the false claim that hormones in contraceptives are harmful, and about 4 in 10 have been exposed to the false idea that hormones in contraceptives limit your ability to get pregnant in the future, according to a new survey.”

item.title: Science News and the Association of Science and Technology Centers Launch Partnership to Bring Science Journalism to More Learners
item.description: Association of Science and Technology Centers: “ASTC is nonprofit network of more than 600 science and technology centers and museums, and allied organizations, engaging nearly 110 million people annually. Through the partnership, ASTC member organizations can provide issues of Science News Explores to their members and donors, as well as student groups, classrooms, field trips, special events and other programs.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: “Finding Their Names” Project Identifies Stories of 4,500 Enslaved Georgians
item.description: University of Georgia: “Names and stories of more than 4,500 Georgians who were enslaved can now be discovered by future generations as part of a University of Georgia Libraries project to discover, digitize, and describe pre-Civil War archival materials.”

item.title: Google Rolls Out September 2026 Spam Update Globally
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “Google has started rolling out the September 2026 spam update, its fourth spam update of the year. The update began Sept. 24 at 9:15 a.m. PDT, according to Google’s Search Status Dashboard. It applies globally and to all languages.”

item.title: How to turn your old Windows PC into a Chromebook for free
item.description: Engadget: “Historically, the only way to access ChromeOS was to buy a Chromebook with it pre-installed. But that changed a few years ago when Google introduced ChromeOS Flex, an official way to install the operating system on your own hardware. The process only takes about an hour, and you may already have everything you need to get started.”

item.title: This free website turned me into a channel surfer again without a streaming app
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Now I either open an app because I already know what I want to watch or spend five minutes scrolling through recommendations until every thumbnail starts looking the same. famelack brought back some of that old channel-surfing chaos. You open a globe, pick a place, and see what turns up. I expected a clever way to peek at live TV from other countries, but I ended up hopping around with no destination in mind and enjoying the randomness enough to keep going far longer than I planned.”

item.title: Vanderbilt Libraries’ ‘Year to Unplug’ seeks to cultivate connection, campus culture of reading
item.description: Vanderbilt University: “While digital technology may be a useful, enjoyable and integral part of campus life, the Jean and Alexander Heard Libraries are inviting Vanderbilt community members to reconsider their relationship with screens this academic year, especially during their down time. The Heard Libraries, in collaboration with key university partners, are making 2026–27 the Year to Unplug—a sustained, institution-wide effort to cultivate a campus culture of reading, reflection and community.”

item.title: ‘WWE Main Event’ Moves From YouTube to Rumble, a Conservative Streaming Platform Backed by JD Vance
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Starting Oct. 14, WWE Main Event is tagging out of the YouTube ecosystem and strutting down the entrance ramp to Rumble — a video-sharing platform and cloud provider that is a favorite of conservative commentators like Dan Bongino, Steven Crowder and Andrew Tate, the journalist Glenn Greenwald, and gamer Dr. Disrespect.”

item.title: US government seeks to join Elon Musk in challenge against EU’s fine on X
item.description: Reuters: “The US government said on Thursday it had formally sought to join a legal challenge filed by billionaire Elon Musk to dismiss a fine of €120 million ($136.51 million) by the European Union against ​his social media platform X. EU tech regulators fined X late last year for breaching ​online content rules, the first sanction under a landmark legislation that has ⁠drawn criticism from Washington.”

item.title: This GTA V mod lets you destroy Flock cameras. Its creator explains why.
item.description: Mashable: “A new Grand Theft Auto V mod from artist Morry Kolman, who goes by WTTDOTM online, installs 235 virtual Flock license plate reader cameras around the game’s fictional city. Called Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, or GTALPR, it brings an extra layer of surveillance to your next drive. And because this is GTA, you can destroy the cameras and collect in-game cash from their wreckage.”

item.title: New York sues prediction market Polymarket, calling it an unlicensed gambling operation
item.description: Associated Press: “New York sued the prediction market Polymarket on Thursday, arguing the platform is an unlicensed gambling operation and calling for a judge to block the company from operating in the state.”

item.title: Saskatoon museum joins global coalition dedicated to Ukrainian studies
item.description: CTV News: “The Ukrainian Museum of Canada has joined the Global Coalition of Ukrainian Studies, an international network dedicated to preserving and sharing knowledge about Ukraine and its cultural heritage. The milestone comes as the museum celebrates 90 years since it was founded by Ukrainian women in Saskatoon.”

item.title: Building a Test Palisade: Learning How Forts Disappear
item.description: Ohio History Connection: “While archaeologists spend much of their time studying what survives in the ground, it is equally important to understand what happens when structures decay. This project is designed to examine how wooden fortifications deteriorate over time and what evidence they leave behind in the archaeological record. The goal is to create a reference collection of known post-depositional processes and feature formation that can be compared to excavated palisade features at Fort Laurens and other eighteenth-century military sites.” Good morning, Internet…
